title: Chaos and Inaction: Former Staffers Accuse Commerce Department under Lutnick of Undermining AI Chip Enforcement
snippet: Former Commerce Department officials allege that under Secretary Howard Lutnick, internal chaos, purges of key experts, and a freeze on blacklisting suspicious firms allowed billions in illicit U.S. microchips to reach China.
content:
Former Commerce Department officials are raising alarms over Secretary Howard Lutnick’s leadership, describing an agency crippled by chaos, micromanagement, and a persistent failure to stop the illegal flow of advanced artificial intelligence chips to foreign adversaries like China.

Key national security responsibilities—such as investigating export ban violations and adding suspected shell companies to the U.S. Entity List—came to a near-total standstill under Lutnick, according to former department officials speaking on condition of anonymity.

A Freeze on National Security Enforcement

Former staffers revealed that an entire year passed without a single company being added to the Entity List, marking the first such enforcement gap in 18 years. Federal Register records confirm no additions were made after October 9, 2025. Even when agency enforcement officers uncovered suspicious activity surrounding Nvidia chip deliveries at Southeast Asian sites, department directors allegedly took no action.

The enforcement breakdown occurred as massive quantities of sensitive technology slipped through the cracks. A study by research nonprofit Epoch estimated that between 290,000 and 1.6 million cutting-edge AI chips were smuggled into China across 2024 and 2025. Furthermore, at least $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia hardware allegedly reached Chinese entities via connections linked to Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese agent whose affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang led to his recent resignation.

Brain Drain and Internal Bottlenecks

Sources attribute the policy collapse in part to an early purge of seasoned career experts. Shortly after Lutnick took office, the department let go of 30-year veteran Matthew Borman, who served as principal deputy assistant secretary for export administration, and Eileen Albanese, longtime director of the Office of National Security Controls. Their departures sparked an exodus of up to 50 senior scientists, engineers, and diversion experts, leaving key leadership roles in the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) completely unfilled.

Remaining staff described severe operational bottlenecks under BIS chief Jeffrey Kessler, whom former employees accused of micromanaging routine decisions while blocking enforcement actions against suspected chip smugglers. Career workforce members reported feeling stymied, often learning about major policy shifts—such as permitting sales of Nvidia's H20 and H200 chips to China—through media reports rather than internal channels.

Public Backlash Within the Cabinet

Criticism of the Commerce Department's inaction has spilled into the open, drawing fire from key administration leaders. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent publicly voiced frustration, telling CNBC that Commerce failed to follow through on chip ban enforcement supported by Treasury, the State Department, and explicit directives from President Trump.

Although the Commerce Department recently issued a new rule requiring export licenses for transferring advanced semiconductors to countries like Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand to curb illicit rerouting, Commerce acknowledged its own role was minimal, noting the regulation was written by the Treasury Department and the National Security Council.
